history.dynasty: Nawab of Farrukhnagar (building originally a mosque, 18th century); converted 1947
history.period: Mosque c. 18th century (exact construction date undocumented); converted to mandir-gurdwara in 1947
history.summary: The Sitaram Temple of Farrukhnagar is a CONVERTED MOSQUE, not an originally Hindu temple. The local Jama Masjid on the town's main street was turned into a mandir and gurdwara in 1947, when the local Muslims migrated and Punjabi refugees settled in the town (Rana Safvi; Outlook Traveller). The three-domed mosque structure survives, with the doorway now carrying the sign 'Shri Sita Ram Mandir - Gurudwara'; it is dedicated to Rama-Sita while also serving as a Gurdwara. Farrukhnagar itself was established in 1732 by Faujdar Khan, first Nawab of Farrukhnagar, governor of Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar, and flourished on the salt trade. CAUTION: this is a different building from the town's other, still-standing Jama Masjid built by Faujdar Khan in red sandstone; the exact construction date of this particular local masjid is not documented.

town_description: Farrukhnagar is a historic Mughal-era town in Gurugram district, Haryana, established in 1732 by Faujdar Khan, first Nawab of Farrukhnagar, and named for Emperor Farrukhsiyar. It flourished on the salt trade until British taxation crippled it in the late 19th century. Its octagonal old town holds the Sheesh Mahal palace, the Ghaus Ali Shah stepwell, Sethani Ki Chhatri, havelis and a heritage railway station (Delhi-Rewari branch, 1873) that still hosts the Fairy Queen run.
tradition: Hinduism (Vaishnavism); also serves as a Gurdwara
